label: paragraph_title
text: WANT MORE PAY.

label: text
text: SOME CANTON RATEWAY WORKKR

label: text
text: K.C.R.—CHINESE BACTION.

label: text
text:
The demand for an increase of wages by the Canton. Kowloon Railway workers was forwarded to the Railway Authorities for over a fortnight. Proposals were made by representatives from both parties.
A reply was recently given by the Railway authorities to the workers saying that owing to financial stringency the railway cannot meet the demands of the workers, for while the railway may easily make promises it will not be able to carry them out. Besides, the demands for a reply in so short a time means danger to the welfare of the railway.
In response, a letter was addressed to the Railway authorities yesterday (says Monday's "Canton Guiehte") by the workers stating, "With regard to financial stringency, the Kwangtung Yuch Hani Railway and the Canton Samshui Railway are in worse condition than the Canton Kowloon Railway, yet the wages of the workers of these two railways are nearly double that of ours. We do not see the reason why you cannot meet the demand of the workers while other railways can. As to the limit of time for a reply from you, our subject is to get an early settlement. There is nothing threatening in it."

label: text
text: It is said that the workers are preparing to take other measures to urge an early settlement, as they regard the attitude of the Railway Authorities as insincere.

label: text

label: paragraph_title
text: HOLLAND'S OUTLOOK

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: The Hague, Sept. 15.

label: text
text:
In her speech from the throne at the opening of the new session of the States General, the Queen declared that in many respects the country had reason to be grateful as the position of agriculture and horticulture was generally satisfactory, though the future outlook was not so bright.
Commerce and industry were still beset with difficulties largely owing to economic conditions outside Holland. The general situation was somewhat improved though there was still ground for anxiety.

label: text
text: The danger disturbing the State's financial resources was past. Thanks to the radical measures adopted the financial situation continued to develop favourably and a reduction of burdens might shortly be considered, but the most sober administration of the State's finances was still imperative.

label: text
text:
Holland's relations with foreign Powers were most cordial and efforts would be immediately made to gradually reduce Holland's military forces compatibly with the international situation. Measures were being considered for the establishment of a Department of National Defence to which the interests of the army and navy would be entrusted so far as it did not concern the Colonies Department.
As regards the colonies the influx of capital was essential to meet this growing needs of the people, but care must be taken that the interests of the native populations were not adversely affected.

label: paragraph_title
text: HISTORIC JERBA

label: text
text: The discovery of a submerged city in the hoard channel separating Jerbin from the miniland of Africa is likely to make the majority of readers inquire—where is Jerbin? It is certainly one of the least known of the islands of the Mediterranean, and very few Englishmen have ever set foot upon it, writes Major Gordon Home in the "Daily Telegraph."

label: text
text: I was there for some time when I was endeavouring to reach Tripoli by means of coasting vessels and Arab feluncens, and although I reached the low sandy island without great difficulty, to leave it was by no means easy unless one chartered a native sailing boat and ran all sorts of chances of being becalmed off a most inhospitable shore or storm-bound in some equally deserted spot.

label: text
text: On the shores of Jerbin near the place where the city has been found are the remains of a Roman port known as Meninx. No excavation has yet been carried out, but finely-scriptured Roman capitals and here and there bases of columns are to be seen placed casually among the handful of "low houses forming the modern village of El Kantam. This name is the Arabic for "The Bridge." for it was here that the Roman Cuusway, of which some remains exist to-day, crossed the shallow strait. Only in the centre of the channel is there any depth of water, for on the three occasions when I have sailed to or from the island I noticed that the boat was often churning up the sand with its keel, and the bottom is visible almost everywhere.

label: text
text: It is therefore clear that a very slight subsidence of the coast would place the lower sandy shore below the level of the sea. That this sinking of the coast has affected the shores of Africa between Cape Bon (north of Tunis) and the Gulf of Gubes, in which Jerba is situated, is fairly plain from the fact that a portion of ancient Carthage is now submerged. And such an alteration in levels is not in any way surprising when one remembers the seismic energy which has throughout the whole historic period caused frequent disturbance in this central portion of the Mediterranean. As recently as 1891 a submarine volcano produced an island (known as Graham's Island) between Sicily and the African coast. Previously there had been a depth of 100 fathoms at the spot, and as the peak rose 200ft. above the sea a cone of volcanic debris some 800ft. in height had been produced. The action of the sea soon reduced the island to a rest, and even that has disappeared, but that such violent disturbances occur is ample explanation for the slight subsidence of the adjoining coast.

label: text
text: The question of the age of this submerged city is one which a close examination of the spot may settle. That it is of great antiquity is probable, for a number of reasons. Jerba has preserved its present name certainly since the time of Aurelius Victor, who wrote about A.D. 370, and it may have been ancient then. Very few names, particularly of islands, changed during the Gracco-Roman period. Then there is the name of Meninx borne by the Roman town known to have existed at this spot, traces of which, as just mentioned, are still to be seen on the island. It is a name suggesting great possibilities of exceptional antiquity, and does not appear to be Greek or Latin in form. It may be Phoenician, but there is some possibility of its being of Minoan origin, and if so the sea may give up long-buried secrets of a colony of this very early civilization. The fact that a vessel stated to be of Grecian origin has been found lying across one of the streets of the city suggests that the earth movement which caused the submergence occurred before that galley with its cargo of vases was sunk. Jerba has always been associated with the land of the Lotos-Eaters, and readers of Homer will recall the lines of the Odyssey.

label: paragraph_title
text: "NEW THRILL."

label: text
text: DEAD MAN'S NAME STOLEN.

label: paragraph_title
text: AMAZING LETTER.

label: text
text: The police have issued a warrant for the arrest of Philip Knapp, a deserter from the United States Army's Flying Corps, on the charge of murdering Louis Panella, a taxi-cub driver, in order to obtain a new thrill out of life by taking Panella's name, and identity. Knapp is a member of a wealthy New York family.

label: text
text: Panella disappeared from his home in Hempstead, Long Island, on July 1, and his dead body was found three days later buried beneath a pile of wood near Mitchellfield flying grounds, Long Island, where Knupp was stationed.

label: paragraph_title
text: UNURIBD FOOT.

label: text
text: The discovery was made accidentally owing to a foot sticking out from the debris. Investigation disclosed that Knapp took three days' leave from barracks on July 1, and when he failed to return his locker was searched, and a remarkable unsigned letter found there.

label: text
text: It was headed "Disappearance of Philip Knapp" and addressed to Knapp's father and Captain Drayton, of the Flying Corps, declaring that Knapp enlisted to escape his wife and obtain a new thrill, the writer desiring to seek the most dangerous undertakings.

label: text
text:
The letter continued: "He tried everything possible, including racing accidents and aeroplane crashes. Boot-legging proved too tame. Six months' jaunt at sea did not involve the desired risks. Self-destruction had been considered, but although the result was desirable, any excitement or enjoyment of facing death was absent.
"What will be done next will be done unknown to all. An absolutely different name will be used, and in this large world the utter impossibility of detection is evident.

label: paragraph_title
text: "ABNORMAL MIND."

label: text
text: This condition of mind is admitted to be most abnormal. Some years back the writer suffered from the effects of a fractured skull. A subsequent operation may have excited all these qualities of irresponsibility. It may be self sufficiency, it may also be—but be what it may, the fact remains that (his name) will cease to exist.

label: text
text: "When he decides to quit this field—it may be within a week or a month—this letter will be held in readiness for that day, for now he has definitely decided in his mind that there is no alternative left."

label: text
text: The police throughout the country have been asked to search for Knapp. A special watch is being kept at all ports.

label: text
text: The results of the inquiry into the causes of Germany's military collapse in 1918 have been presented to the members of the Reichstag in a monumental work of three volumes, each numbering 1,366 pages.

label: text
text: The Reichstag Commission employed three experts to study the available material and to provide written reports. The three were Professor Hans Delbrück, the historian; Colonel Schwerdtfeger, a writer on military affairs; and General von Kühl, who was chief of staff to Prince Rupprecht and was in close touch with General Ludendorff.

label: text
text: Professor Delbrück blames General Ludendorff for his precipitation at the end of 1918, when, despite the opposition of the Government, he forced Germany to apply for an armistice. He holds that Germany might have made a favourable peace had the General Staff abandoned the idea of anэхing foreign territory.

label: text
text: Colonel Schwerdtfeger arrives at the conclusion that the collapse was not the fault of individuals, but a fate from which there was no escape.

label: text
text: Capt. G. F. Wilkins, leader of the British Museum expedition, which has been two years in Australia, has returned to London. He told a "Daily Mail" reporter how he was able to gain the confidence of cannibal natives in the North-Eastern Territory who had always been hostile to white men.

label: text
text: Captain Wilkins stated that when a party of natives attacked his camp one night he went out carrying a bright light, and the attackers, afraid to throw their spears, disappeared into the bush.

label: text
text: His own native helpers were afraid to go to sleep, and they spent the night telling him of their exploits. In the morning they realised that they had confessed to a great number of crimes, and they no doubt considered that the only way to secure his silence was to tell him other and more dreadful things and take him completely into their confidence.

label: text
text: From these people, he said, he learned a great deal of native lore and customs and this enabled him later to approach the even more aggressive natives of Groote Hyland, who had never before allowed any white man to visit their camp.

label: text
text: Thousands of specimens collected by the expedition will eventually be shown in the British Museum.

label: paragraph_title
text: LEGACY OF ERRORS.

label: paragraph_title
text: MISPRINTS THAT PERSIST IN SHAKESPEARE.

label: text
text: For some years past it has been increasingly recognised in England that anyone who sets out to edit or annotate Elizabethan or Jacobean plays without an adequate knowledge of the handwritings of the period is not likely to do much to improve his author's text. Dramatic texts, including Shakespeare's, despite all the work which has been done on them during the last two centuries, still stand in need of further corrections, because while in other forms of literature many, perhaps most, authors corrected their proofs, most dramatists did not. The main reason for this was, doubtless, that as a rule they had no pecuniary interest in printed editions of their plays, all the rights (as far as the extent evidence shows) having passed to the companies of actors for which the plays were written. Proof-reading in those days, moreover, seems to have involved frequent attendance at the printing house; and for an actor-dramatist, with performances in the afternoon and rehearsals (presumably) in the morning, this would have been especially inconvenient. The blame cast on the printers for the misprints which resulted from their being left to do the best they could is thus largely unjust; but the misprints were made, and undoubtedly many of them still disfigure current texts, some as recognised difficulties and others as poor readings which editors are too conservative to alter.

label: text
text:
If more of the corruptions which still linger in dramatic texts are to be eliminated, emendation must be inspired and controlled by a knowledge (1) of the different kinds of misprints which have already been corrected, (2) of the various ways in which letters were formed, more especially by the dramatist himself, but also by other authors of the period, (3) of the various ways in which words could be spelt.
Dr. Keilner, who has issued a work entitled "Restoring Shakespeare" prefaces it by saying that "from 1914 to this day" he has been "busy to the exclusion of all other work, applying the key of the elizabetthan handwriting to the unexplained passages in Shakespeare's works"; and he ventures a modest hope that as a result of his labours he has "arrived at a number of satisfactory readings."
